claim: Flagella and cilia propel swimming eukaryotic cells and drive fluids on epithelial tissues of higher organisms.
source: Flagella and cilia propel swimming eukaryotic cells and drive fluids on epithelial tissues of higher organisms (Alberts et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alberts et al., 2015

claim: The inner structure of the eukaryotic flagellum is an arrangement of microtubules and accessory proteins called the axoneme.
source: The inner structure of the eukaryotic flagellum is an arrangement of microtubules (MTs) and accessory proteins called the axoneme (Ax).
evidence: Established structural knowledge about eukaryotic flagella

claim: The axoneme typically consists of nine cylindrically arranged MT doublets cross-bridged by motor proteins of the dynein family.
source: A highly conserved structure in evolution, the Ax typically consists of nine cylindrically arranged MT doublets cross-bridged by motor proteins of the dynein family.
evidence: Established structural knowledge about axoneme organization

claim: An internal central pair of MTs is connected by radial spokes to the nine peripheral doublets, determining the typical '9+2' axonemal structure.
source: An internal central pair of MTs is connected by radial spokes to the nine peripheral doublets, determining the typical '9+2' axonemal structure.
evidence: Established structural knowledge about axoneme organization

claim: Motor proteins hydrolyze ATP to generate forces that induce doublet sliding.
source: Motor proteins hydrolyze ATP to generate forces that induce doublet sliding.
evidence: Established knowledge about dynein motor protein function

claim: Dynein-induced sliding of MTs translates into bending movements of the whole structure due to mechanical constraints exerted by linking proteins and the basal body.
source: Due to mechanical constraints exerted by linking proteins (nexins) and the basal body, dynein-induced sliding of MTs translates into bending movements of the whole structure.
evidence: Established knowledge about the sliding-to-bending mechanism in flagella

claim: Motor proteins are thought to self regulate their activity via mechanical feedback, generating the periodic beats of flagella.
source: Motor proteins are thought to self regulate their activity via mechanical feedback, generating the periodic beats of flagella, see, for example, Brokaw, 2009 and Lindemann and Lesich, 2010.
evidence: Supported by citations to Brokaw, 2009 and Lindemann and Lesich, 2010

claim: The inner working of the axoneme is not fully understood and is still the subject of active research.
source: Despite a general consensus on the existence of a self-regulatory mechanism, the inner working of the Ax is not fully understood and it is still the subject of active research (Wan and Jékely, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wan and Jékely, 2020

claim: Bending-through-sliding is the accepted fundamental mechanism of flagellar motility.
source: While bending-through-sliding is the accepted fundamental mechanism of flagellar motility, how specific flagellar shapes are determined is not yet clear.
evidence: Established consensus in the field

claim: How specific flagellar shapes are determined is not yet clear.
source: While bending-through-sliding is the accepted fundamental mechanism of flagellar motility, how specific flagellar shapes are determined is not yet clear.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge

claim: Nodal cilia present in early embryonic development display markedly non-planar beats.
source: Nodal cilia present in early embryonic development display markedly non-planar beats (Buceta et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buceta et al., 2005

claim: For animal sperm cells and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, the flagellar beat is, to a good approximation, planar.
source: On the other hand, for the most studied swimming microorganisms, such as animal sperm cells and the biflagellate alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, the flagellar beat is, to a good approximation, planar.
evidence: Established observational knowledge about these organisms

claim: Beat planarity in sperm cells and Chlamydomonas is thought to be induced by inter-doublet links between MTs 5 and 6.
source: For these organisms, beat planarity is thought to be induced by the inter-doublet links between one pair of MTs, typically those numbered 5 and 6 (Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2012

claim: Inter-doublet links between MTs 5 and 6 inhibit the relative sliding of this MT pair, selecting a beating plane that passes through the center of the axoneme and the midpoint between the inhibited MTs.
source: These links inhibit the relative sliding of the 5-6 MTs pair, thus selecting a beating plane that passes through the center of the Ax and the midpoint between the inhibited MTs.
evidence: Mechanistic explanation based on structural constraints

claim: Euglenids and kinetoplastids have an extra element attached alongside the axoneme called a paraflagellar rod.
source: A remarkable deviation from the flagellar structure of the aforementioned organisms is found in euglenids and kinetoplastids. These flagellated protists have an extra element attached alongside the Ax (Cachon et al., 1988), a slender structure made of a lattice-like arrangement of proteins called 'paraxial' or 'paraflagellar' rod (PFR), see Figure 1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cachon et al., 1988 and reference to Figure 1

claim: The paraflagellar rod is a slender structure made of a lattice-like arrangement of proteins.
source: These flagellated protists have an extra element attached alongside the Ax (Cachon et al., 1988), a slender structure made of a lattice-like arrangement of proteins called 'paraxial' or 'paraflagellar' rod (PFR), see Figure 1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cachon et al., 1988 and reference to Figure 1

claim: PFRs are attached via bonding links to up to four axonemal MTs, depending on the species.
source: PFRs are attached via bonding links to up to four axonemal MTs, depending on the species (Walne and Dawson, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walne and Dawson, 1993

claim: PFRs are thought to be passive, but in Euglena gracilis some degree of activity is not completely ruled out.
source: PFRs are thought to be passive but, at least in the case of Euglena gracilis, some degree of activity is not completely ruled out (Piccinni, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piccinni, 1975

claim: Euglena gracilis has two flagella, designated as dorsal and ventral.
source: E. gracilis has two flagella, designated as dorsal and ventral.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about E. gracilis

claim: The ventral flagellum of E. gracilis remains within the reservoir, an invaginated region of the cell.
source: The ventral flagellum remains within the reservoir, an invaginated region of the cell.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about E. gracilis

claim: The dorsal, PFR-bearing flagellum of E. gracilis emerges from the reservoir and serves as a propulsive apparatus by means of periodic beating.
source: The dorsal, PFR-bearing, flagellum emerges from the reservoir and serves as a propulsive apparatus by means of periodic beating.
evidence: Established anatomical and functional knowledge about E. gracilis

claim: The beating style of E. gracilis is sometimes dubbed 'spinning lasso'.
source: In this paper, we show that the beating style of E. gracilis, sometimes dubbed 'spinning lasso' (Bovee, 1982), is characterized by a distinctive geometric signature, namely, traveling torsional peaks with alternating sign along the length of the flagellum.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bovee, 1982

claim: The beating style of E. gracilis is characterized by traveling torsional peaks with alternating sign along the length of the flagellum.
source: In this paper, we show that the beating style of E. gracilis, sometimes dubbed 'spinning lasso' (Bovee, 1982), is characterized by a distinctive geometric signature, namely, traveling torsional peaks with alternating sign along the length of the flagellum.
evidence: This is a main finding of the paper based on analysis of experimental data

claim: The distinctive beating style of E. gracilis arises from the PFR-Ax mechanical interaction.
source: Moreover, we put forward and test the hypothesis that this distinctive beating style arises from the PFR-Ax mechanical interaction.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis tested in the paper through modeling

claim: The flagellar beat of PFR-bearing kinetoplastid organisms such as Leishmania and Crithidia is planar.
source: In order to put our hypothesis into context, we observe that the flagellar beat of PFR-bearing kinetoplastid organisms, such as Leishmania and Crithidia, is planar (Gadelha et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gadelha et al., 2007

claim: Trypanosoma brucei shows a characteristic non-planar 'drill-like' motion.
source: An apparent exception to beat planarity in kinetoplastids is found in the pathogenic parasite Trypanosoma brucei, which shows a characteristic non-planar 'drill-like' motion (Langousis and Hill, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Langousis and Hill, 2014

claim: It has been claimed that the flagellar structure alone could account for the emergence of T. brucei's drill-like motion.
source: It has been claimed that the flagellar structure alone could account for the emergence this motion (Koyfman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koyfman et al., 2011

claim: The flagellum of T. brucei is attached to the organism for most of its length, wrapped helically around the cell body.
source: However, the flagellum of T. brucei is not free, like that of Leishmania and Crithidia, but it is attached to the organism for most of its length, wrapped helically around the cell body.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about T. brucei

claim: The flagellum-body mechanical interaction can alone explain T. brucei's distinctive motion.
source: According to Alizadehrad et al., 2015, the flagellum-body mechanical interaction can alone explain T. brucei's distinctive motion.
evidence: Supported by citation to Alizadehrad et al., 2015

claim: T. brucei mutants with body-detached flagellum generate fairly planar beating.
source: Confirming this conclusion, Wheeler, 2017 showed that T. brucei mutants with body-detached flagellum generate fairly planar beating.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wheeler, 2017

claim: It is conjectured that the PFR-Ax bonds operate as the 5-6 interdoublet links in Chlamydomonas and sperm cells, inhibiting MTs sliding and selecting a plane of beat.
source: It is conjectured that the PFR-Ax bonds operate as the 5-6 interdoublet links in Chlamydomonas and sperm cells, inhibiting MTs sliding and selecting a plane of beat (Woolley et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Woolley et al., 2006

claim: The spinning lasso beat of E. gracilis does not conform to the scenario of planar beating.
source: The spinning lasso beat of E. gracilis does not conform to this scenario.
evidence: Observational statement contrasting E. gracilis with other organisms

claim: E. gracilis beating style is characterized by high asymmetry and non-planarity.
source: Indeed, E. gracilis beating style is characterized by high asymmetry and non-planarity.
evidence: Observational statement about E. gracilis flagellar beat

claim: The full 3d flagellar kinematics of freely swimming E. gracilis cells has been revealed by Rossi et al., 2017 using a mixed approach based on hydrodynamic theory and image analysis.
source: The full 3d flagellar kinematics of freely swimming cells has recently been revealed by Rossi et al., 2017 thanks to a mixed approach based on hydrodynamic theory and image analysis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossi et al., 2017

claim: The geometry of the spinning lasso is characterized by traveling waves of torsion with alternating sign along the flagellum length.
source: As we report in the first part of this paper, the geometry of the spinning lasso is characterized by traveling waves of torsion with alternating sign along the flagellum length.
evidence: This is a main finding of the paper based on analysis of experimental data

claim: The key to the emergence of non-planarity lies in a prominent structural asymmetry of the PFR-Ax attachment in euglenid flagella.
source: We argue that the key to the emergence of non-planarity lies in a prominent structural asymmetry of the PFR-Ax attachment in euglenid flagella.
evidence: This is the central argument of the paper based on structural analysis

claim: In E. gracilis, the PFR is attached to MTs 1, 2, and 3.
source: The PFR is attached to MTs 1, 2, and 3.
evidence: Based on electron microscopy studies cited in the text

claim: In E. gracilis flagellum, the line connecting the center of the Ax and the center of the PFR crosses the line passing through the center of the Ax and MT 2.
source: The two lines cross each other. This is the structural feature on which we build our model.
evidence: Based on structural analysis from electron microscopy studies and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: The bonding links to the PFR select the local spontaneous beating plane of the Ax from the principle of MTs' sliding inhibition.
source: In modeling the flagellar complex, we assume that the bonding links to the PFR select the local spontaneous beating plane of the Ax, from the same principle of MTs' sliding inhibition discussed above.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on analogy with other systems

claim: Under generic actuation, the two flagellar components (Ax and PFR) cannot be simultaneously in their respective states of minimal energy due to the offset between the spontaneous beating plane of the Ax and the line joining the PFR-Ax centers.
source: We show that, under generic actuation, the two flagellar components cannot be simultaneously in their respective states of minimal energy, and this crucially depends on the offset between the spontaneous beating plane of the Ax (dashed line in Figure 1) and the line joining the PFR-Ax centers (solid line in Figure 1).
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived from the model

claim: The typical outcome of the Ax-PFR interaction is an elastically frustrated configuration in which the two competing components drive each other out of plane.
source: Instead, the typical outcome is an elastically frustrated configuration of the system, in which the two competing components drive each other out of plane.
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived from the model

claim: Under dyneins activation patterns that would produce an asymmetric beat similar to Chlamydomonas or Volvox in the absence of extra-axonemal structures, the model predicts the torsional signature of the spinning lasso.
source: Under dyneins activation patterns that, in the absence of extra-axonemal structures, would produce an asymmetric beat similar to those of Chlamydomonas (Qin et al., 2015), or Volvox (Sareh et al., 2013), the model specifically predicts the torsional signature of the spinning lasso.
evidence: This is a main theoretical prediction of the model, with citations to Qin et al., 2015 and Sareh et al., 2013

claim: The lack of symmetry of the spinning lasso beat produces swimming trajectories with rotations coupled with translations.
source: Interestingly, the lack of symmetry of the spinning lasso beat produces swimming trajectories with rotations coupled with translations (Rossi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossi et al., 2017

claim: Cell body rotations have a key role in the light-guided navigation behavior of phototactic unicellular organisms.
source: In turn, cell body rotations have a key role in the light-guided navigation behavior of phototactic unicellular organisms (Goldstein, 2015), and of E. gracilis in particular, which has recently attracted renewed attention (Giometto et al., 2015; Ogawa et al., 2016; Tsang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goldstein, 2015; Giometto et al., 2015; Ogawa et al., 2016; Tsang et al., 2018

claim: Rotations along the major axis of the cell body produced by the spinning lasso beat allow the light-sensing apparatus of E. gracilis to constantly scan the environment and align with light intensity gradients.
source: Rotations along the major axis of the cell body produced by the spinning lasso beat allow the light-sensing apparatus of the organism to constantly scan the environment, and align E. gracilis with light intensity gradients.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of the spinning lasso beat

claim: The beat of the euglenid flagellum can be seen as an example of a biological function arising from the competition between antagonistic structural components.
source: In light of these observations, our analysis shows that the beat of the euglenid flagellum can be seen as an example of a biological function arising from the competition between antagonistic structural components.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis in the paper

claim: The 'spinning lasso' exhibits torsion peaks of alternate sign that travel from the proximal to the distal end of the flagellum.
source: The 'spinning lasso' exhibits here a distinct torsional signature: torsion peaks of alternate sign that travel from the proximal to the distal end of the flagellum.
evidence: This is an observation from analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Torsion is the rate of change of the binormal vector and measures the deviation of a curve from a planar path.
source: Torsion, the rate of change of the binormal vector, is the geometric quantity that measures the deviation of a curve from a planar path (see the 'Results' Section below for the formal definition).
evidence: This is a mathematical definition from differential geometry

claim: Flagellar non-planarity in E. gracilis is not intrinsically associated with swimming.
source: While with fixed specimens we cannot reconstruct reliably the 3d flagellar shapes, Figure 3 shows that there is a high stereographical consistency with the flagellar shapes obtained from swimming organisms. Flagellar non-planarity is thus not intrinsically associated with swimming, which reinforce the idea that the mechanism that generates non-planar flagellar shapes might be structural in origin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of trapped and swimming cells, with reference to Figure 3

claim: The 2d outline of a beating euglenid flagellum is typically that of a looping curve.
source: Typically, the 2d outline (i.e. the projection on the focal plane) of a beating euglenid flagellum is that of a looping curve, see Figure 3 and, for example Tsang et al., 2018 for independent observations.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 3 and supported by citation to Tsang et al., 2018

claim: A curve with two singular points of concentrated torsion with opposite sign generates a looping curve when seen in two-dimensional projection.
source: When seen in a two-dimensional projection, the torsion dipole generates a looping curve, which closely matches euglenid flagella's outlines during a spinning lasso beat.
evidence: This is a geometric analysis relating 3D torsion to 2D projections

claim: The axoneme is the only active component of the flagellum, whereas the PFR is purely passive.
source: We suppose that the Ax is the only active component of the flagellum, whereas the PFR is purely passive.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated in the paper

claim: The PFR's bending and twisting stiffness are neglected in the model.
source: We are neglecting here the PFR's bending and twisting stiffness.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated in the paper

claim: Bending and twist moduli scale with the fourth power of the cross section radius, whereas shear and stretching moduli scale with the second power.
source: Classical estimations on homogeneous elastic rods, see, for example Goriely, 2017, show that bending and twist moduli scale with the fourth power of the cross section radius, whereas shear and stretching moduli scale with the second power and hence they are dominant for small radii.
evidence: Supported by citation to Goriely, 2017

claim: The twistless nature of axonemal deformations is fundamentally a consequence of the fact that shear of axonemal MTs and twist are uncoupled.
source: This is, fundamentally, a consequence of the fact that shear of axonemal MTs and twist are uncoupled (Equation 6).
evidence: This is an explanation based on the kinematic constraints in the model

claim: MTs' sliding stretches the Ax-PFR bonding links, which inhibits sliding of MTs 1, 2, and 3, and triggers a dynein organization similar to that in Chlamydomonas.
source: Our working hypothesis is that MTs' sliding stretches the Ax-PFR bonding links, which, in turn, inhibits sliding of MTs' 1, 2, and 3, and triggers a dynein organization (via mechanical feedback) similar to the one present in Chlamydomonas.
evidence: This is a working hypothesis stated in the paper

claim: If the Ax-PFR joining line is neither parallel nor orthogonal to the spontaneous bending plane of the Ax, then the emergent flagellar shapes are non-planar.
source: We can prove analytically the following statement: if the Ax-PFR joining line is neither parallel nor orthogonal to the spontaneous bending plane of the Ax, then the emergent flagellar shapes are non-planar.
evidence: This is an analytical result proven in the paper

claim: The model is able to reproduce the experimentally observed flagellar beats and the characteristic geometric signature of spinning lasso.
source: The model is able to reproduce the experimentally observed flagellar beats and the characteristic geometric signature of spinning lasso, namely, traveling waves of torsion with alternating sign along the length of the flagellum.
evidence: This is a main result of the paper comparing model predictions with experimental observations

claim: The peculiar non-planar shapes of the beating flagellum of Euglena gracilis arise from the mechanical interactions between the axoneme and the paraflagellar rod.
source: We show that the peculiar non-planar shapes of its beating flagellum, dubbed 'spinning lasso', arise from the mechanical interactions between two of its inner components, namely, the axoneme and the paraflagellar rod.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper stated in the abstract

claim: The spontaneous shape of the axoneme and the resting shape of the paraflagellar rod are incompatible.
source: The spontaneous shape of the axoneme and the resting shape of the paraflagellar rod are incompatible.
evidence: This is a key concept in the model stated in the abstract

claim: The complex non-planar configurations of the coupled Ax-PFR system emerge as the energetically optimal compromise between the two antagonistic components.
source: Thus, the complex non-planar configurations of the coupled system emerge as the energetically optimal compromise between the two antagonistic components.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the paper stated in the abstract

claim: The fluid-structure interaction does not disrupt the Ax-PFR structural incompatibility.
source: Indeed, the fluid-structure interaction does not disrupt the Ax-PFR structural incompatibility, which still generates non-planar shapes with traveling waves of torsional peaks with alternating sign and the typical looping-curve outlines, Figure 2.
evidence: This is a result from hydrodynamic simulations shown in Figure 7

claim: The unique flagellar beat of E. gracilis produces the typical roto-translational trajectories of swimming cells.
source: The unique flagellar beat of E. gracilis is at the base of the distinctive behavior of the organism, producing the typical roto-translational trajectories of swimming cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by swimming simulations

claim: Swimming simulations using experimentally measured flagellar shapes with Resistive Force Theory demonstrate that the flagellar beat produces roto-translational trajectories.
source: This has been demonstrated by swimming simulations using the experimentally measured flagellar shapes in Rossi et al., 2017 with a Resistive Force Theory approach to model hydrodynamic interactions between the cell and the surrounding fluid.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossi et al., 2017

claim: Swimming simulations using theoretical waveforms produced by the model generate swimming paths similar to typical observed trajectories.
source: We carried out here analogous simulations using the theoretical waveforms produced by our model. The application of Resistive Force Theory hydrodynamics to the waveforms shown in Figure 7 produces swimming paths similar to the typical observed trajectories.
evidence: This is a result from swimming simulations shown in Figure 8

claim: In swimming simulations, the cell is propelled by the flagellum, following a generalized right-handed helical trajectory while rotating around its major axis.
source: The cell is propelled by the flagellum, following a generalized right-handed helical trajectory while rotating around its major axis.
evidence: This is a result from swimming simulations shown in Figure 8

claim: After each full turn of the helix, the cell completes one full body rotation.
source: After each full turn of the helix the cell completes one full body rotation.
evidence: This is a result from swimming simulations shown in Figure 8

claim: The origin of the peculiar shapes of the euglenid flagellum can be explained by the mechanical interplay of two antagonistic flagellar components, the Ax and the PFR.
source: We have shown how the origin of the peculiar shapes of the euglenid flagellum can be explained by the mechanical interplay of two antagonistic flagellar components, the Ax and the PFR.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the paper stated in the Discussion

claim: The conclusions are based mainly on the hypothesis that sliding inhibition by the PFR organizes dynein activity and localizes the spontaneous bending plane of the Ax.
source: Our conclusions are based mainly on the hypothesis that sliding inhibition by the PFR organizes dynein activity, and localizes the spontaneous bending plane of the Ax as the one that passes from the Ax center through the MTs bonded to the PFR.
evidence: This is a statement about the basis of the conclusions in the paper

claim: The hypothesis of PFR-mediated sliding inhibition is in agreement with the current understanding of the mechanism that generates beat planarity in other PFR-bearing flagellar systems.
source: This is in agreement with the current understanding of the mechanism that generates beat planarity in other PFR-bearing flagellar systems.
evidence: This is a statement relating the hypothesis to existing knowledge

claim: Non-planarity in E. gracilis can arise because of a marked asymmetry in the Ax-bonding links-PFR complex in the euglenid flagellum, which is not found in kinetoplastids.
source: Non-planarity in E. gracilis can arise because of a marked asymmetry in the Ax-bonding links-PFR complex in the euglenid flagellum, which is not found in kinetoplastids such as Leishmania (Gluenz et al., 2010) or Trypanosoma (Portman and Gull, 2010).
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the paper with citations to Gluenz et al., 2010 and Portman and Gull, 2010

claim: The emergent distortion of the Ax generated by the Ax-PFR interplay could in principle lead to different actuation patterns, consistently with the hypothesis of dynein actuation via mechanical feedback.
source: We appreciate that the emergent distortion of the Ax, generated by the Ax-PFR interplay, could in principle lead to different actuation patterns, consistently with the hypothesis of dynein actuation via mechanical feedback.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential extensions of the model

claim: Including dynein feedback in the euglenid flagellum model could potentially open new avenues for the study of ciliary motility in general.
source: Including dynein feedback in the euglenid flagellum model we proposed will require further study, and can potentially open new avenues for the study of ciliary motility in general.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions

claim: The structural and kinematic peculiarities of the E. gracilis beat may provide a challenging new model system to test the relative merits of alternative theories of mechanical feedback in flagella.
source: The structural and kinematic peculiarities of the E. gracilis beat may provide a challenging new model system to test the relative merits of these alternative theories.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential value of E. gracilis as a model system

claim: The spinning lasso produces the typical roto-translational motion of E. gracilis cells.
source: Along with the mechanism that let the euglenid flagellar shapes emerge, it is worth considering how this characteristic flagellar beat is integrated in the overall behavior of the organism. The spinning lasso produces the typical roto-translational motion of E. gracilis cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional consequence of the spinning lasso beat

claim: Cell body rotation in E. gracilis is associated with phototaxis.
source: Cell body rotation is in turn associated with phototaxis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. gracilis behavior

claim: Rotation allows E. gracilis cells to veer to the light source direction when stimulated, or escape in the opposite direction when the signal is too strong.
source: Indeed, rotation allows cells to veer to the light source direction when stimulated, or escape in the opposite direction, when the signal is too strong.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. gracilis phototactic behavior

claim: Periodic signals generated by lighting and shading associated with body rotations are used for navigation, as the existence of periodicity implies a lack of proper alignment.
source: Here, the key biochemical mechanism could be the one often found in nature, by which periodic signals generated by lighting and shading associated with body rotations are used for navigation, in the sense that the existence of periodicity implies a lack of proper alignment (Goldstein, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goldstein, 2015

claim: The PFR is directly connected with the light-sensing apparatus in E. gracilis.
source: It is known that the PFR is directly connected with the light-sensing apparatus (Rosati et al., 1991), and might even be contractile (Piccinni, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rosati et al., 1991 and Piccinni, 1975

claim: Transient light stimuli have been shown to change flagellar beat patterns in E. gracilis.
source: Transient light stimuli have been shown to change flagellar beat patterns.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. gracilis behavior

claim: The euglenid flagellum consistently presents looping outlines, but its extension from the cell body changes with changing light intensity signals, resulting in a variety of 'quantized' phototaxis behaviors.
source: While the euglenid flagellum consistently present looping outlines (the 2d trace of a torsion dipole), its extension from the cell body changes with changing light intensity signals, resulting in a variety of 'quantized' phototaxis behaviors (Tsang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsang et al., 2018

claim: E. gracilis is a unicellular organism exhibiting a variety of motility behaviors including flagellar swimming and metaboly.
source: Our results confirm, however, the interest of euglenids as model systems for responsive unicellular organisms: E. gracilis, in particular, is a unicellular organism exhibiting a variety of motility behaviors (flagellar swimming and metaboly, see Leander et al., 2017) and capable of responding to a variety of stimuli, from light to confinement, see Noselli et al., 2019.
evidence: Supported by citations to Leander et al., 2017 and Noselli et al., 2019

claim: E. gracilis is capable of responding to a variety of stimuli, from light to confinement.
source: E. gracilis, in particular, is a unicellular organism exhibiting a variety of motility behaviors (flagellar swimming and metaboly, see Leander et al., 2017) and capable of responding to a variety of stimuli, from light to confinement, see Noselli et al., 2019.
evidence: Supported by citations to Leander et al., 2017 and Noselli et al., 2019

claim: Strain SAG 1224-5/27 of Euglena gracilis was obtained from the SAG Culture Collection of Algae at the University of Göttingen.
source: Strain SAG 1224-5/27 of Euglena gracilis obtained from the SAG Culture Collection of Algae at the University of Göttingen was maintained axenic in liquid culture medium Eg.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental materials

claim: An Olympus IX 81 inverted microscope with motorized stage was employed in all the experiments.
source: An Olympus IX 81 inverted microscope with motorized stage was employed in all the experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental equipment

claim: Micrographs were recorded at a frame rate of 1,000 fps with a Photron FASTCAM Mini UX100 high-speed digital camera.
source: Micrographs were recorded at a frame rate of 1,000⁢fps with a Photron FASTCAM Mini UX100 high-speed digital camera.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental equipment and settings

claim: Cells were immobilized at the tip of the capillary by applying a gentle suction pressure via a syringe connected to the capillary by plastic tubing.
source: Cells were immobilized at the tip of the capillary by applying a gentle suction pressure via a syringe connected to the capillary by plastic tubing.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental procedure

claim: The observations reported in this paper are restricted to specimens with immotile cell bodies, in absence of metaboly.
source: The observations reported in this paper are restricted to specimens with immotile cell bodies, that is, in absence of metaboly.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the selection criteria for observations

claim: The absence of metaboly suggests minimal impact on cell behavior in response to capillary entrapment.
source: The absence of metaboly also suggests minimal impact on cell behavior in response to capillary entrapment.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental conditions
